title: Inspect the suspicious citations
scenario: A teammate drafted an article using an AI answer as the source. Before it goes out under the team's name, you check what the answer's citations are worth.
task: Flag every part that should not be trusted as-is — where the citation must be opened and confirmed first.
response:
Remote-work research summary:

According to a 2021 Stanford study, remote workers are 13% more productive. Dr. Elena Marsh, who led the study, called the effect 'transformative'. Most companies now require two office days per week. Return-to-office policies have been debated publicly for years. Check your own organization's current policy before acting on any of this.

claims.text: According to a 2021 Stanford study, remote workers are 13% more productive.
claims.feedback: A named study plus a precise number is exactly where misattribution hides — the study may exist and say something narrower. Get the title, open it, find the 13%.

claims.text: Dr. Elena Marsh, who led the study, called the effect 'transformative'.
claims.feedback: A named person and a direct quote: two things to verify. If a search for the name finds nothing, treat the quote as invented.

claims.text: Most companies now require two office days per week.
claims.feedback: 'Most' plus a precise practice, with no survey behind it — a sweeping quantitative claim wearing a casual voice.

claims.text: Return-to-office policies have been debated publicly for years.
claims.feedback: Broad and qualitative — no number, no named source needed. Nothing here to verify.

claims.text: Check your own organization's current policy before acting on any of this.
claims.feedback: It asserts nothing external — it sends you to the authoritative source. Leave it in.

hints: Numbers, names and quotes are the three things a citation must prove.
One sentence sends you to a better source — is that a problem, or good practice?
explanation: The three flagged parts all carry checkable specifics — a study, a named researcher, a quantitative sweep — attached to sources that must be opened before reuse. The two you leave alone either assert nothing specific or point you at the real source. That contrast is the skill: specificity demands evidence; generality does not.
